title: Romantic Expressionism

jokes.text: Did you slip out for a quickie with Prof. Hot Stuff? / There's a gold star on your fly.
jokes.setup: Someone asks Jeff if he snuck away for a quickie with Professor Michelle.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's fly has a gold star sticker on it — physical evidence left by the professor confirming the encounter.
jokes.explanation: Economical and sharp cold open — the visual punchline (gold star on the fly) is a perfectly specific, unexpected image that confirms the tryst without stating it. The 'gold star for good work' double meaning is tight. Strong structure for an opener.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: How did you know about that?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: The evidence is literally stuck to your pants.

jokes.text: Why is Annie talking to Micro-Nipples?
jokes.setup: Vaughn is introduced as a shirtless, spiritual hippie type playing guitar for Annie.
jokes.punchline: Jeff dismissively refers to him only by a physical characteristic — 'Micro-Nipples' — refusing to even use his name.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Jeff — dismissive, reductive, and absurdly specific. 'Micro-Nipples' as a nickname for a shirtless guy is brilliantly petty and character-specific. The refusal to use Vaughn's name reads as jealousy wrapped in contempt, which is exactly Jeff's mode. High quotability, great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, is that a gold star on my... Oh my God. This is amazing. This is the kind of recognition I deserve.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Finally, someone understands me. A gold star. The highest honor.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm framing this. This goes in my office. Next to my law degree.

jokes.text: He never wears a shirt. He never wears shoes. Why hasn't he died from lack of service?
jokes.setup: Troy observes that Vaughn perpetually violates the 'no shirt, no shoes, no service' rule.
jokes.punchline: Extends the logic to its absurd conclusion — interpreting 'lack of service' as literally fatal rather than merely inconvenient.
jokes.explanation: Classic Troy logic — takes a mundane observation and follows it to a gloriously literal, surreal conclusion. The rhythm of three short sentences is tight. Very Troy-specific in its earnest absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: Okay, so this is a basic D chord. But it's not just any D chord—it's a D chord that represents the duality of man's struggle against the cosmos.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: Feel the chord. Really feel it. Your fingers are touching the strings, but your soul is touching the universe.

jokes.text: Kickpuncher starring Don 'The Demon' Donaldson as a cyborg cop whose punches have the power of kicks.
jokes.setup: Abed invites Troy to watch a movie in his dorm tonight.
jokes.punchline: The movie concept is so perfectly, specifically terrible — a cyborg cop whose special power is that his punches feel like kicks, the most modest superpower imaginable.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the specificity — 'whose punches have the power of kicks' is an absurdly minimal superpower, which makes the B-movie parody land perfectly. Abed's deadpan delivery of this as a fully serious film synopsis is very character-integrated. This is the seed of a running gag that pays off throughout the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Vaughn, you know what? I'm breaking up with you.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: What? Why?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Because you're just abs. You're not a person, you're just abs with a head attached.

jokes.text: That sounds awful. / I'll bring the popcorn.
jokes.setup: Britta correctly identifies Kickpuncher as an awful movie.
jokes.punchline: Troy immediately volunteers to attend anyway, treating the awfulness as the draw.
jokes.explanation: Quick, functional beat. The rhythm works — Britta's judgment vs. Troy's enthusiasm — but it's fairly standard sitcom shorthand for 'these guys like bad movies.' Not especially novel.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: No wait, G could also stand for... you know, the universe, or like, energy, or whatever. It's all connected, man. The G chord is just one expression of the infinite cosmic vibration.

jokes.text: Shirley, don't embarrass yourself. I'm sure they don't want to invite the housewife.
jokes.setup: Shirley seems interested in joining the movie night.
jokes.punchline: Pierce tries to 'protect' Shirley by being inadvertently condescending and sexist, calling her 'the housewife' as if that disqualifies her.
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce — his attempts to help are more offensive than doing nothing. 'The housewife' is a perfectly oblivious label. The humor comes from his total lack of self-awareness rather than wit. Functional character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: No shirt, no shoes, no service. That's like... the ultimate rejection, man. It's society saying you're not worthy of existing in their space.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: It's a dress code for restaurants, Vaughn.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: Exactly. They're telling me I can't even eat. I can't sustain myself. I'm being slowly erased from civilization, one barefoot step at a time.

jokes.text: Actually, if she doesn't mind reinforcing the stereotype, I bet Shirley would have fun talking smack in a movie.
jokes.setup: Pierce has just condescended to Shirley.
jokes.punchline: Jeff corrects Pierce while simultaneously making his own backhanded assumption about Shirley — that she'd be good at 'talking smack' — which is its own kind of stereotype.
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Jeff's 'correction' of Pierce contains its own racial assumption, and Jeff is barely aware of it. The self-awareness is the point. Good character work for Jeff — his wokeness is always slightly performative.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: In this movie, every time someone gets punched, they get kicked instead.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It makes no logical sense, but that's the whole point.

jokes.text: Pierce, you don't wanna watch a cyborg movie in Abed's dorm. You wanna lay in your twin bed and think about what you used to be.
jokes.setup: Pierce tries to invite himself to movie night.
jokes.punchline: Jeff delivers a genuinely cruel but funny image — Pierce alone in a twin bed, contemplating lost youth — with complete casual confidence.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's cruelty is always most effective when it's specific and bleak. 'Think about what you used to be' is a sharp image with real bite. The 'twin bed' detail elevates it from generic insult to precise, sad picture.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's terrible, but I'm going to enjoy it anyway.

jokes.text: What, you think I'm too old to make monkeyshines at a picture show? / Come on, I'm younger than the three of you put together.
jokes.setup: Jeff implies Pierce is too old to enjoy the movie night.
jokes.punchline: Pierce uses an absurdly antiquated phrase ('monkeyshines at a picture show') and then follows with mathematically questionable bragging about his age.
jokes.explanation: 'Monkeyshines at a picture show' is pitch-perfect Pierce — out-of-date slang delivered with total confidence. The follow-up claim that he's 'younger than three of you put together' is absurd self-delusion that characterizes Pierce beautifully.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: You know, I normally have much better sense than this. But I figure if I'm going to have the full college experience, I might as well do something stupid with my friends.

jokes.text: You know, everyone talks about his nipples, but his feet freak me out.
jokes.setup: The group has been discussing Vaughn's shirtlessness and 'micro-nipples.'
jokes.punchline: Britta pivots from the established joke to an entirely different physical concern — his feet — which reframes the whole discussion.
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-timed pivot. The callback structure works because it acknowledges the conversation has evolved, then subverts it. Britta being weirded out by feet rather than nipples is a small character note.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Can I join you guys for movie night?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Why don't you go contemplate your mortality instead?

jokes.text: Annie haltingly trying to confess she hasn't kissed Vaughn yet — 'We haven't... Anything.' — while Britta's reaction lands as a silent beat.
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to ask Britta's permission to date Vaughn and has to admit they haven't been physical at all.
jokes.punchline: The stammering — 'We haven't... Anything' — lands as awkward, innocent vulnerability that is both endearing and funny, especially against Britta's experienced composure.
jokes.explanation: Character-specific cringe. Annie's nervous innocence contrasted with Britta's worldliness is a consistent comic dynamic. The fragmented dialogue is well-written even if it's not a big laugh moment.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: That's cool, that's cool. I'm still young. I'm down with the kids. I know all the latest slang. That's fly, that's tight, that's off the hook.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: And I'm not old—I'm only 65 times 2.

jokes.text: You're the coolest girl I've ever met. / Damn right, give me some fivesies. / Turning it into a snake.
jokes.setup: Annie sincerely compliments Britta as a cool older woman.
jokes.punchline: Britta's immediate 'Damn right' + 'fivesies' + 'turning it into a snake' shows her trying extremely hard to be cool in a way that undermines the compliment.
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Britta's desperate need to be seen as 'the cool girl' causes her to overperform coolness the moment someone calls her cool. 'Fivesies' and 'turning it into a snake' are perfect details — slightly dated, slightly tryhard. Very character-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: His nipples are weird.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: No, like, his butt has a weird shape.

jokes.text: She asked for my blessing. / And you gave it? / Yeah, I'm done with him.
jokes.setup: Jeff is horrified Britta gave Annie permission to date Vaughn.
jokes.punchline: Britta's reasoning — 'I'm done with him' — reveals she only said yes because she no longer wants Vaughn, not out of any real generosity.
jokes.explanation: Quick, efficient character reveal. Britta's 'I'm done with him' as her entire reasoning is a good deflation of her earlier 'coolest girl' self-image. Not a big laugh but plants the seed for the later jealousy revelation.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, you didn't know Vaughn was in a band?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I knew he was *in* a band. I just didn't know which one.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Or what instruments they played.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Or what their music sounded like.

jokes.text: And it all starts with Vaughn. He's a gateway douche bag.
jokes.setup: Jeff argues that Vaughn, while harmless, represents a dangerous precedent for Annie's taste in men — 'creepier and creepier dudes' will think she's available.
jokes.punchline: 'Gateway douche bag' — borrowing the drug escalation metaphor to describe men who lead to worse men.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. 'Gateway douche bag' is an inspired coinage — it repurposes the 'gateway drug' concept with perfect economy to make a simultaneously funny and somewhat valid social observation. It's entirely Jeff: confident, analytical, and self-serving. Became a cultural touchstone line from this episode. High originality, perfectly economical.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Vaughn is so sweet.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh, Vaughn? Yes, well, he was a simpler time. A more innocent era. We don't speak of those days anymore.

jokes.text: And that can be your toast at her shotgun wedding to Star-Burns.
jokes.setup: Britta defends a fatalistic, 'people collide, things happen' philosophy.
jokes.punchline: Jeff projects her philosophy to its logical endpoint — Annie in a shotgun wedding to Star-Burns (a minor recurring character known only for his elaborate sideburns) — as a devastating hypothetical.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Star-Burns' as the endpoint of Annie's romantic decline is brilliant — using a known recurring character for maximum comedic effect. 'Shotgun wedding toast' as the framing for Britta's nihilism is sharp and character-integrated. Excellent structure.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Troy, you don't understand. When you tried to ask me out, I thought you were someone else.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: What? Who did you think I was?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I don't know, someone taller. Someone with better shoes. Someone who wasn't you.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's... that's just mean.

jokes.text: Oh, now turn to your right. Yes, we can see both of them. It's like a constellation on your face.
jokes.setup: Star-Burns (the character with elaborate star-shaped sideburns) is the subject of discussion immediately after Jeff name-drops him.
jokes.punchline: Cut to someone examining Star-Burns' face — his sideburns are so extravagant that two people need to view them from different angles, 'like a constellation.'
jokes.explanation: The cut to Star-Burns right after the reference is good structural timing. 'It's like a constellation on your face' is a solid visual description of absurd facial hair. The juxtaposition — Jeff mentions him, we immediately see him being examined — is a nice editing joke.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: No, it wouldn't bug me at all. Why would it bug me? I'm over Vaughn. I'm completely over him, which I am not.

jokes.text: That guy over there? He's a douche bag.
jokes.setup: Jeff spots someone (likely Vaughn) across the room.
jokes.punchline: Jeff delivers a completely unprompted, blunt assessment to no one in particular — a callback to 'gateway douche bag' compressed to two words.
jokes.explanation: Brief, effective punctuation to the previous scene. Jeff is now just pointing at Vaughn and issuing verdicts. Economical character beat — we understand his fixation.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Thank you so much, Britta!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: No problem. Hey, let's seal it with our special handshake.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: *attempts elaborate handshake that devolves into an awkward snake motion*

jokes.text: I hope you don't mind I invited Señor Chang, we're Netflix friends. / Oh, that's cool you're hanging out, drinking beers with your students. / Yeah, clearly none of my other plans fell through.
jokes.setup: Abed has invited their Spanish teacher, Señor Chang, to movie night.
jokes.punchline: Jeff sarcastically notes the inappropriateness of a teacher socializing with students; Chang responds with brutal self-awareness — 'clearly none of my other plans fell through' — confirming the pathetic subtext.
jokes.explanation: Chang's self-aware admission that this is his social life by default is a great character moment. 'Netflix friends' as a descriptor of the teacher-student relationship is perfectly clinical and funny. The exchange builds well: Abed is guileless, Jeff is sarcastic, Chang is devastatingly honest.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: It's cute that Annie and Vaughn are together.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Explain to me what's cute about it.

jokes.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Shirley. I'll wait if you wanna serve beverages. / You're going to be waiting a long ass time.
jokes.setup: Pierce makes a condescending assumption that Shirley, as the housewife, should be serving drinks.
jokes.punchline: Shirley refuses to take the bait with magnificent bluntness — 'a long ass time.'
jokes.explanation: The Pierce-Shirley dynamic is reliable — his oblivious sexism vs. her dignified pushback. 'A long ass time' lands with good timing and character specificity for Shirley, whose mild profanity always has comedic value.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Britta, you need to stop encouraging Annie to date Vaughn. He's a groovy hipster and she deserves better.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Says the guy wearing a polo shirt and gel in his hair.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: This is classic. Timeless.

jokes.text: Oh, FBI warning, I'm so scared.
jokes.setup: The movie starts with the standard FBI anti-piracy warning.
jokes.punchline: Pierce mock-sarcastically reacts to the FBI warning with exaggerated fear, the most predictable possible riff.
jokes.explanation: This is the joke that establishes Pierce's attempt to be the funniest in the room — but the FBI warning joke is deliberately weak/hacky. The meta-point is that Pierce thinks this is good material, which is funnier than the joke itself. Scores low as a standalone joke, but serves the larger narrative function.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Dating Vaughn is like a gateway drug. You start with him, and pretty soon you're dating guys who are way worse.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's not how gateway drugs work.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Isn't it? You start with weed, next thing you know you're doing heroin.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's literally the opposite of what happens with dating.

jokes.text: Hey, that's not fair. I didn't know we started.
jokes.setup: Pierce missed the FBI warning joke being made.
jokes.punchline: Pierce treats the movie riffing as a competitive sport with formal start rules — 'I didn't know we started' — revealing his pathological need to win.
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Pierce is approaching casual fun with the competitive seriousness of a sporting event. The 'I didn't know we started' line treats something informal like a formal competition, which is very Pierce.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So you're saying that I'm your gateway douche bag? Like, I'm gonna lead you to worse and worse guys until you end up pregnant at Star-Burns' wedding?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's not what I said.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No, no, I get it. It's like a gateway drug, but with douchebags. First it's me, then it's someone slightly worse, then it's someone even worse, and eventually you're knocked up at Star-Burns' shotgun wedding, wearing a dress you bought at a gas station.

jokes.text: Sounds like a Thanksgiving at my house.
jokes.setup: Movie narration describes a post-apocalyptic world of 'scavengers, drug dealers and terrorists.'
jokes.punchline: Shirley compares it to her Thanksgiving — implying her family gatherings are that dysfunctional.
jokes.explanation: Classic movie riffing joke — the setup is handed to them by the film. Shirley's self-deprecating family angle fits her character. The timing appears good and it's the first sign she's good at this.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Star-Burns, your face is like a constellation.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: People come from all over just to see it.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: It's basically a national landmark at this point.

jokes.text: They just come to me.
jokes.setup: Troy makes a joke during the movie riffing ('Troy, you're crazy, man').
jokes.punchline: Troy responds with total false modesty — 'They just come to me' — as if his comedic genius is beyond his control.
jokes.explanation: Troy's earnest self-regard is always funny. 'They just come to me' in four words establishes that Troy considers himself naturally gifted without any performance or irony. Very economical characterization.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Look at him. That's a guy in a bowler hat with stars shaved into his head. He's not a rebel, he's not a pioneer—he's a cautionary tale.

jokes.text: Will it get me through this movie? / There she goes. Shirley's in the house.
jokes.setup: Movie drug dealer asks 'You want to buy some megadope? It gets you mega high.'
jokes.punchline: Jeff riffs: 'Will it get me through this movie?' — which Shirley tops, prompting Troy to announce her arrival as a riffing presence.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's riff is functional movie-mockery; the real joke is Troy's sports-announcer reaction to Shirley's good line. The sequence establishes that Shirley is unexpectedly excellent at this.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Dude, you can't just hang out with us. You're a teacher. That's like... that's weird and sad.

jokes.text: Freeze police? Don't do that, they'll get cold.
jokes.setup: Movie cop shouts 'Freeze, police!'
jokes.punchline: Shirley mishears 'Freeze' as an adjective modifying 'police' — the police themselves are being told to freeze — 'they'll get cold.'
jokes.explanation: Clean wordplay — reinterpreting 'freeze police' as 'freezing the police' is a solid grammatical misdirect. The delivery likely sells it. Good example of Shirley's unexpected comedic ability.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: This is my backup plan. I was gonna be a dancer.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Now I'm a security guard hanging out with students. It's sad, but it's what I got.

jokes.text: Yeah, two hours of my life back.
jokes.setup: Movie hero is asked 'Is there anything we can give you?' as a reward.
jokes.punchline: Jeff riffs as the hero: 'Two hours of my life back' — the standard 'this movie is a waste of time' joke.
jokes.explanation: Very well-worn movie riffing joke — 'I want my time back' — but the setup is perfectly timed. Gets the job done but no originality points.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Shirley, why don't you serve the beverages? That's what the woman does.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: 'Directed by Kim Yang.' / Asian, can't direct, can't drive.
jokes.setup: Movie credits show the director's name, Kim Yang.
jokes.punchline: Pierce delivers an enthusiastically racist joke, oblivious to Abed sitting right next to him.
jokes.explanation: The joke isn't the racism — it's Pierce's total unawareness that Abed is right there. 'Dude, I'm right here' is the actual punchline. The racism itself is deliberately hacky and old; the comedy is in Pierce's obliviousness. Character-integrated but the underlying 'joke' Pierce tells is intentionally bad.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: This is a federal crime warning. They're coming for me. I knew it would happen eventually.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: All those things I did in the '70s... they finally caught up with me.

jokes.text: Dude, I'm right here. / Right there.
jokes.setup: Pierce makes a racist joke about Asian people without registering Abed's presence.
jokes.punchline: Abed's 'Dude, I'm right here' and Pierce's confirmation 'Right there' — with no apparent remorse, just acknowledgment.
jokes.explanation: The two-word exchange is perfect. 'Right there' as Pierce's entire response — confirming he heard Abed, confirming he doesn't care — is devastating in its brevity. This is excellent economy and character work: Abed's flat delivery vs. Pierce's complete moral vacancy. The structure builds over two beats with perfect timing. Genuinely exceptional exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I didn't notice the apocalypse.

jokes.text: Well, actually, tomorrow we— / No. / We were all gonna get— / I wouldn't. / Right? / Tomorrow night, we're all gonna get together and watch Kickpuncher 2: Codename Punchkicker.
jokes.setup: Various people start to suggest plans for tomorrow that the group can tell will be bad ideas.
jokes.punchline: Abed steamrolls everyone's objections to announce Kickpuncher 2 with complete conviction, having already decided.
jokes.explanation: The title 'Kickpuncher 2: Codename Punchkicker' is a brilliant joke in itself — the sequel simply reverses the words, which is a perfect parody of action sequel naming. Abed's unilateral declaration despite everyone's hesitation is well-characterized.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: That's just like my family gatherings.

jokes.text: Well, I was warming up tonight. Tomorrow you better foam the runways because I'm bringing my A game.
jokes.setup: Pierce has been making mediocre jokes all night. Everyone agrees to a Kickpuncher 2 sequel night.
jokes.punchline: Pierce treats the casual movie-riffing like a competitive sporting event requiring runway foam — the metaphor is both grandiose and wrongly applied.
jokes.explanation: 'Foam the runways' as a sports/warfare metaphor for watching a bad movie is wonderfully disproportionate. Pierce's self-seriousness about his comedic ability when we've seen how bad it is creates the irony. Good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Well, I'm definitely gonna need those drugs to get through this movie.

jokes.text: He's got her in some kind of hippie collar. / I can hear her armpit hair growing from here.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Britta watch Annie do a surfing lesson with Vaughn on campus.
jokes.punchline: Two rapid-fire observations about how thoroughly Annie has been absorbed into Vaughn's hippie world — 'hippie collar' and 'armpit hair growing' are vivid, nasty images.
jokes.explanation: 'Hippie collar' as a description of Vaughn's embrace, and the specific detail of audible armpit hair growth, are vivid and sharp. Britta's line is particularly good — she's mocking the hippie lifestyle she once embraced, adding a layer of self-aware irony.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! Are you okay? You're freezing! Here, take my jacket.

dialogue.speaker: Police Officer
dialogue.line: Freeze! Police!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm serious, man. You're shivering. Do you need a blanket? Some hot cocoa?

jokes.text: Let's just center ourselves. There it is.
jokes.setup: Jeff is trying to come up with a scheme; Britta says they should 'center themselves' (using yoga/hippie language).
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'There it is' — pointing out that Britta has already adopted Vaughn's hippie vocabulary without realizing it.
jokes.explanation: 'There it is' as a two-word indictment is brilliantly economical. Jeff catching Britta saying something Vaughn-esque and simply noting it rather than arguing is a mature comedic choice. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Movie Character
dialogue.line: What can we give you?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I want the time I spent watching this returned.

jokes.text: This problem won't respond to tap dancing or casual revelations that you spent time in New York.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Britta are trying to 'hatch a scheme' and Jeff is dismissing what he anticipates Britta's contributions will be.
jokes.punchline: Jeff lists Britta's specific, useless skill set — 'tap dancing' and 'casual revelations that you spent time in New York' — as her go-to moves for solving problems.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character specificity. 'Casual revelations that you spent time in New York' is a perfectly observed Britta tic — the kind of thing a character does that you don't realize until someone names it and it immediately becomes definitive. This line could ONLY be about Britta. 'Tap dancing' as her other useless skill is absurd and funny. High originality, strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Kim Yang? That's a Chinese name, right? I bet he makes great movies... and great lo mein!

jokes.text: Okay, if you're gonna get Upper East Side about this, I think we're done.
jokes.setup: Jeff accuses Britta of being New York-pretentious; she responds by calling HIM Upper East Side — New York's most elite neighborhood.
jokes.punchline: Britta fights back using the same geographic snobbery she was just accused of, completely undermining her position.
jokes.explanation: Britta inadvertently proves Jeff's point by deploying New York geography as an insult. The irony is that she escalates the exact behavior she's being called out for. 'Upper East Side about this' is a great turn of phrase.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You just said that in front of me.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: What? No, I didn't.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You did. You literally just said it.

jokes.text: Hey, Winger, check out Annie. / Somebody just went to the top of my to-do list.
jokes.setup: Someone points Jeff toward Annie (who is looking attractive while with Vaughn).
jokes.punchline: Jeff's immediate sexualization — 'to-do list' as both literal task list and crude double entendre — reveals his interest in Annie.
jokes.explanation: 'To-do list' as a crude double entendre lands medium well. The irony that Jeff was just discussing Annie's well-being and now views her as a prospect is a good character moment. The joke itself is not especially original.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'll be back tomorrow night, and I promise you, the comedy will be nothing short of a smooth landing.

jokes.text: Okay, we need to hatch a scheme. / Thank you.
jokes.setup: Jeff spent the whole previous scene trying to convince Britta to scheme; she resisted. After Jeff's 'to-do list' moment, she suddenly agrees.
jokes.punchline: Britta's motivations shift from protecting Annie to jealousy; Jeff's 'Thank you' acknowledges the hypocrisy of both their positions.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's flat 'Thank you' — acknowledging the moment without comment — is a great understated beat. The whole structure of this scene is economical: they both flip their positions the moment personal jealousy enters the picture. Good writing.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh no. Oh no no no. Annie, what is happening? What happened to you? You look like a Stevie Nicks fever dream. Did Vaughn do this to you? Of course he did. Look at him, he's like if a guitar had a face and the face made poor life choices. You're hanging out with him and now you're dressed like you're about to teach a pottery class to unemployed people. I can literally hear your hair growing. That's not a metaphor, I can actually hear it. It's making a sound. It's like a soft whooshing noise, like wind through a very dumb forest.

jokes.text: Chemistry, sexy. You know what else is sexy? Annie.
jokes.setup: Jeff is 'manipulating' Troy by working Annie's attractiveness into a conversation about Chemistry class.
jokes.punchline: The segue is transparently, comically bad — 'Chemistry, sexy. You know what else is sexy? Annie.' — a fake non-sequitur.
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Jeff, who just spent a confessional explaining sophisticated manipulation theory ('you help them realize they want to do it'), executes the most clumsy, obvious maneuver imaginable. The gap between his self-image as a master manipulator and his actual technique is the core comedy of this whole subplot. Very well-structured irony.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Scheming isn't really my wheelhouse.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No, your wheelhouse is more like... saying something weird, immediately regretting it, and then overexplaining it until everyone's uncomfortable.

jokes.text: She had braces and acne and a pill addiction. A nervous breakdown ending with her running through a plate glass door screaming: 'Everyone's a robot.'
jokes.setup: Jeff asks Troy to describe Annie from high school.
jokes.punchline: Troy escalates from normal teenage awkwardness (braces, acne) to pill addiction to a full nervous breakdown involving a plate glass door and the belief that everyone is a robot.
jokes.explanation: The escalation structure is excellent — braces and acne are relatable, pill addiction is a jump, then 'plate glass door' and 'everyone's a robot' is a full comic detonation. The specificity of 'everyone's a robot' as her breakdown manifesto is inspired. This is well-structured dark comedy that also retroactively adds depth to Annie's character.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh, that's rich coming from you, Jeff. You're like the Upper East Side of people.

jokes.text: Troy, I want you to clear your head. / Done.
jokes.setup: Jeff sets up his manipulation technique — 'clear your head.'
jokes.punchline: Troy's instant 'Done' — delivered with complete confidence and no apparent thought — reveals a mind that was already essentially empty.
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-beat exchange. Jeff asks Troy to clear his mind as a rhetorical setup; Troy treats it as a literal instruction and executes immediately. 'Done.' is one of the best Troy jokes in the episode — it implies he had nothing in his head to clear. Maximum economy (one word punchline), perfect character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Whoa, Annie! Looking good! You know, if you weren't a student here, I'd... well, let's just say I'd have to check your ID first.

jokes.text: Ahem. And she's Jewish?
jokes.setup: Jeff is describing Annie's attractiveness. Troy's reaction has been building.
jokes.punchline: Troy's 'And she's Jewish?' — delivered as if Jewishness is an unexpected added bonus, the final item on a checklist of desirable qualities — is an absurd, specific, funny non-sequitur.
jokes.explanation: The 'And she's Jewish?' punchline is funny because of its specificity and total non-sequitur quality — it implies Troy has an unexpected and unexplained thing for Jewish women, presented with complete earnestness. The 'ahem' before it suggests polite inquiry. Great economy and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay Troy, I need your help with something. Now, I'm going to use a technique called 'flattery.' See how I'm about to compliment you? 'You're the only person I trust.' Classic. Then I'll create artificial scarcity: 'I can only ask you because everyone else is too busy or incompetent.' And finally, the false choice: 'So will you help me, or will you let me down?' Notice how I've eliminated the option of you saying no?

jokes.text: Oh wait, never mind, it's too late. I heard she's hooking up with Vaughn. / Only to make you jealous. / What? / She's helplessly in love with you, she's only with Vaughn to get your attention. / And you have to give it to her now, right Jeff? / Sure. / But the point is we're not telling you what to do.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Britta are manipulating Troy by using classic reverse psychology — first making Annie seem available, then making her unavailable.
jokes.punchline: Jeff and Britta's ham-fisted 'we're not telling you what to do' after explicitly and in detail telling him exactly what to do.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the gap between Jeff's earlier description of sophisticated manipulation and what we're watching — a totally transparent, laughably obvious scheme that Troy falls for anyway. The 'we're not telling you what to do' is a great button.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Why don't you see Annie as attractive?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Well, she's got a weird baby face. Her neck is too long. She dresses like a first-grader. And sometimes when she laughs, I think about my dad.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Also, her voice makes me want to die. Not in a good way. In a bad way. In a way where I actively consider driving my car off a bridge.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Plus there's something about the way she moves that makes me think about death. Not my death. Everyone's death. The heat death of the universe.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: And sometimes I see her and I just think about how one day we're all going to be dust, and nothing matters, and God is dead, and I'm pretty sure it's because of her face.

jokes.text: Boo-ya. / I have the weirdest boner.
jokes.setup: Movie moment — Kickpuncher returns from apparent death.
jokes.punchline: Pierce's non-sequitur confession — 'I have the weirdest boner' — delivered presumably with complete sincerity in response to the action sequence.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on Pierce-character level — he's 60+ years old unironically announcing his arousal at a cyborg movie. The 'weirdest' qualifier implies even he doesn't fully understand his own reaction. The juxtaposition with 'Boo-ya' is perfect setup. Very economical.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: She's smart, she's determined, she's got a great work ethic...

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Is she...is she mixed?

jokes.text: All right, guys, you hear that pause after he says, 'And a good day for'? What do you got for me there?
jokes.setup: Movie leaves a rhetorical pause after 'And a good day for—'
jokes.punchline: Pierce soliciting suggestions from the group, coaching them like a comedy director, reveals that he has been preparing this whole operation and now needs content.
jokes.explanation: Pierce treating the casual movie riffing as a managed creative production is excellent character comedy. His solicitation of 'material' shows he has no actual comedy instinct, only process.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Okay, so I used to date this guy who was really into Annie types, and he told me the only way to get their attention is to seem dangerous and unpredictable.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: So what you need to do is start talking about your time in prison.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I've never been to prison.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Not with that attitude. Look, I'll help you. I was in a gang in Portland.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You were not in a gang.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: A small gang. We mostly just did psychological warfare. Anyway, the point is, you need a dark past.

jokes.text: It's a good day for a terrible movie. / It's a good day for hair products?
jokes.setup: Pierce has asked the group to pitch him joke completions for 'It's a good day for—'
jokes.punchline: Jeff and Britta's suggestions are both deliberately weak — not for the movie riff, but as a commentary on the exercise itself.
jokes.explanation: These jokes are deliberately bad — they're not meant to be funny but to illustrate that the group is barely trying for Pierce. Scores low as jokes but serve the meta-narrative.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, Annie likes me? Annie?!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Oh no. Oh no, oh no, oh no.

jokes.text: Oh, Buzz, how many times can you keep going to that well?
jokes.setup: Someone (likely Jeff/Chang) suggests a Buzz Aldrin reference.
jokes.punchline: Pierce critiquing someone else's joke as repetitive when his own material has been entirely hacky.
jokes.explanation: Pierce being a comedy critic despite being the worst comedian in the room is good irony. His standards for others vs. himself is a consistent character note.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Okay, here's how you make a movie joke. You need a setup, a misdirect, and then you hit them with the punchline. It's like a three-act structure, but funny.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: See, most people don't understand the science of comedy. There's a precise moment when you deliver the joke. Too early, they don't get it. Too late, they've already moved on.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You gotta target the funny bone like it's a data point on a graph. Comedy is a discipline.

jokes.text: Come on, guys, I'm starting to wonder if you deserve to call yourselves a community college sketch comedy troupe.
jokes.setup: Pierce has been demanding professional-grade material from the group for a movie riffing session.
jokes.punchline: 'Community college sketch comedy troupe' — the insult he deploys is itself self-deflating; calling them a 'community college' troupe as the lowest bar only highlights where they all are.
jokes.explanation: Meta-joke on Community's own premise — the insult 'community college sketch comedy troupe' is the show commenting on itself. Pierce using his most withering criticism only reveals his own context. Good meta-awareness without being too cute.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm tired of these amateur hour jokes. There should be standards. There should be an organization that oversees comedy quality.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm talking about the International Bureau of Comedic Excellence. IBCE. They would have regulations, certifications, the whole nine yards.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: And frankly, all of you would fail the entrance exam. Spectacularly.

jokes.text: What are you, my third wife's therapist?
jokes.setup: Someone asks Pierce if he wouldn't rather just watch the movie and have a good time.
jokes.punchline: 'My third wife's therapist' — the detail that it's the THIRD wife is a small, devastating backstory joke revealing the wreckage of Pierce's romantic life.
jokes.explanation: The joke does a lot of work in a small space. 'Third wife's therapist' implies: (1) multiple marriages, all of which ended badly enough to require therapy; (2) Pierce has been through this lecture enough times to recognize it; (3) all three wives apparently had the same therapeutic concerns about him. Highly character-specific and economical.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm telling you, the comedy standards have really dropped. You know who had it right? Gallagher. That man knew how to entertain. He'd smash a watermelon, and people would laugh for days. Now what do we get? Some guy talking about his feelings for twenty minutes.

jokes.text: What if he said, 'It's a good day for,' and you said, 'For being gay?'
jokes.setup: The group has been struggling to come up with a joke completion for the movie pause.
jokes.punchline: Chang suggests a simple, juvenile gay joke — which Pierce finds genius.
jokes.explanation: The joke isn't the content — it's that Pierce finds it brilliant. The humor is in Pierce and Chang's shared lowbrow sensibility, not the joke itself. The gay joke is deliberately hacky; the joke IS that it's hacky and they don't know it.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Just relax and have fun.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: That's what my marriage counselor said. Look how that turned out.

jokes.text: You are a genius. / He likes gay jokes. / What? I said we write great jokes. / Don't flatter yourselves.
jokes.setup: Pierce declares Chang a genius for a hacky gay joke; Jeff notes the real dynamic.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'He likes gay jokes' as a clinical diagnosis; Pierce's 'Don't flatter yourselves' — somehow turning the meta-observation into a denial.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's flat 'He likes gay jokes' as an anthropological observation is very Jeff — stripping away Pierce's delusion with a simple diagnosis. Pierce's indignant 'Don't flatter yourselves' is a great non-sequitur denial.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I need better jokes from you people. Step it up.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: What did the chicken say when it crossed the road?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I don't know, what?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: It crossed the road.

jokes.text: Oh, I don't know where Abed is. I can try calling him if you want. / No, I'm not looking for my other half.
jokes.setup: Troy approaches Annie. She assumes he's looking for Abed because they're always together.
jokes.punchline: 'I'm not looking for my other half' — Troy's protest implicitly confirms the Troy/Abed pairing is so established that people assume they're one unit, while also being slightly insulted by it.
jokes.explanation: Sweet joke about the Troy/Abed relationship — the fact that they've become so inseparable that people assume they travel as a unit. 'My other half' is a romantic term applied to a friendship, with slightly uncomfortable implications.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: That's gold, Jerry! Gold!

jokes.text: I'm looking for you, girl. / Oh. / Yeah, let that sink in for a second.
jokes.setup: Troy is deploying Jeff's manipulation — trying to make Annie feel desired.
jokes.punchline: 'Yeah, let that sink in for a second' is hilariously over-coached — a smooth-talker phrase that is not smooth at all, delivered as a literal instruction.
jokes.explanation: 'Let that sink in for a second' as a literal pause instruction during a romantic overture is a perfect comedy line. It signals that Troy has memorized steps from somewhere ('I'm looking for you, girl' also sounds rehearsed) but has no instinct for how to actually perform them. The line is very quotable, deeply character-specific, and the timing is perfect. Excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You're looking for Abed?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: What? No, I... I was actually looking for you.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Me?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Yeah, I was wondering if maybe you wanted to, uh, get some lunch or something? Just the two of us?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Troy, are you asking me out?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I mean, only if you want to. No pressure or anything. I just think you're really cool and smart and... yeah.

jokes.text: Sorry it took me so long. They made me find a s-shirt.
jokes.setup: Vaughn arrives wearing a shirt — apparently for the first time — apologizing for the delay.
jokes.punchline: He had to be 'made' to wear a shirt, and the implied visual of Vaughn in his shirt (combined with his slight stammer on 's-shirt' as if the word is unfamiliar to him) is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff to the 'no shirt, no shoes' thread. Vaughn being coerced into a shirt and his slight verbal stumble on the word suggests it's a foreign object to him. Character-specific and well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Annie, I've been thinking about us, and I really think we could—

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Troy, no.

jokes.text: Hi, bro. / I'm not your bro, bro. / Oh, well, actually, everyone is my bro in the whole entire universe because everything is connected. Rocks, eagles, hats.
jokes.setup: Troy is trying to be intimidating/competitive with Vaughn over Annie.
jokes.punchline: Vaughn's spiritual philosophy, applied to the confrontation, results in 'rocks, eagles, hats' as his examples of universal brotherhood — the list ending on 'hats' is an absurd anticlimax.
jokes.explanation: 'Rocks, eagles, hats' as the list exemplifying universal connection is inspired. The anticlimax of 'hats' after the grandeur of 'rocks, eagles' deflates the whole spiritual speech. Troy's 'I'm not your bro, bro' is also a great immediate self-contradiction.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Bro, bro, bro!

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: Whoa, man. You know, the word 'bro' is just a social construct. We're all connected on this planet, brother. We're all one consciousness experiencing itself subjectively. Except for toasters, spatulas, and those little clips that hold bags of bread closed.

jokes.text: Yeah, but some things are more connected than others, like tarantulas and me peeing my pants.
jokes.setup: Vaughn claims everything in the universe is connected.
jokes.punchline: Troy counters with a highly specific personal example — the connection between tarantulas and his involuntary urination — which is simultaneously philosophical AND reveals a personal trauma.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. Troy accidentally makes a philosophically valid point (Hume's causation!) while revealing a specific embarrassing personal history. The logic is impeccable: tarantulas and his involuntary bodily response ARE strongly correlated. The specificity is perfect — Troy Barnes would absolutely have a tarantula-related pants-wetting incident. High originality, great character integration, deeply quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: Everything is connected, man. We're all just vibrations in the universe.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's beautiful, Vaughn. But I gotta be honest with you - I'm terrified of balloons. Like, irrationally terrified. I once cried at a birthday party for forty-five minutes because someone brought a helium balloon shaped like a giraffe. I still have nightmares about it.

jokes.text: Or me and Annie.
jokes.setup: Troy has just made his 'tarantulas and peeing my pants' connection; now pivots to claim a similar strong connection with Annie.
jokes.punchline: The juxtaposition of 'tarantulas causing me to urinate' and 'me and Annie' as equivalent examples of strong connection is inadvertently insulting.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the previous joke. By following 'tarantulas and me peeing my pants' with 'or me and Annie,' Troy has categorized his feelings for Annie alongside a phobia-induced incontinence response. The logic is consistent and the implication is hilarious. Excellent structure.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: Wait, Annie loves you? Like, for real?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Yeah, man.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: Wow. That's beautiful, bro-ski.

jokes.text: You swear? Like Britta swore that she didn't like Jeff. Then gave him a copy of my poem so he could laugh at me with that Sherri Shepherd lady?
jokes.setup: Annie swears her feelings for Troy are over. Vaughn pushes back.
jokes.punchline: Vaughn reveals a specific grievance — Britta sharing his private poem with Jeff — and identifies Jeff's companion as 'that Sherri Shepherd lady' (not knowing her name), suggesting he's been hurt and obsessively reconstructed the event.
jokes.explanation: 'That Sherri Shepherd lady' is a great detail — Vaughn knows this was a specific person but doesn't know her name, only her general type. The fact that he has stored this grievance with this level of detail is funny and sad. Good callback to series continuity.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: My feelings for Troy are completely over.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: Yeah, well Britta read my poetry to people at parties without asking me.

jokes.text: It's happening again. / Your study group is evil. / And you don't deserve ice cream.
jokes.setup: Vaughn is upset that the study group has manipulated Annie's relationships again.
jokes.punchline: 'And you don't deserve ice cream' — Vaughn's most devastating condemnation is denying Annie dessert, revealing the limits of his threat repertoire.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The escalation sets up something serious ('your study group is evil') and the punchline deflates it completely — Vaughn's ultimate punishment is ice cream denial. It's a perfect window into his character: sincere, gentle, non-threatening, and somewhat ridiculous. 'You don't deserve ice cream' has become one of Community's more quotable lines. Excellent structure and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: Wait, you guys set this whole thing up? You manipulated me?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Welcome to the study group, Vaughn.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: This is unbelievable. What kind of punishment could possibly fit this betrayal?

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: We're banning you from the ice cream social.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: No. No! Not the ice cream social!

jokes.text: Well, he's a baby. Now, where were we?
jokes.setup: Vaughn has stormed off in upset after the confrontation.
jokes.punchline: Troy's instant dismissal — 'he's a baby' — and immediately refocusing on his seduction of Annie is tone-deaf and funny.
jokes.explanation: Troy's total unawareness of the emotional chaos he's just caused, pivoting immediately to his romantic objectives, is good character work. Economical and in character.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Why would you do that?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Annie, you're like a fine cut of meat. You've got good marbling, you're tender, and you're worth every penny.

jokes.text: Ugh! I like him. Why would you do that? / Come on, everybody knows you want a cut of the T-Bone steak.
jokes.setup: Annie is furious that Troy blew up her relationship with Vaughn.
jokes.punchline: Troy's 'everybody knows you want a cut of the T-Bone steak' — referring to himself in the third person as a steak — is both oblivious and gloriously vain.
jokes.explanation: Troy referring to himself as 'the T-Bone steak' is wonderfully self-aggrandizing and ridiculous. The food metaphor applied to himself reveals both his vanity and his slightly odd relationship with language. Very character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Annie wants me now? Annie wants... me? I'm gonna need a cold shower. Actually, I'm gonna need a series of cold showers. Like, a schedule of cold showers.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Troy, that's concerning.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: No, it's fine. I'm just gonna sit in an ice bath. For like a week.

jokes.text: Oh, you're even hotter when you're angry. / Let's do this. / Red Shoe Diaries. / I think you know I have a thing for butt stuff.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Britta are caught having plotted together; Annie is furious. Jeff makes it worse by flirting.
jokes.punchline: The scene cuts to Jeff and Britta in celebration mode — 'Let's do this' — then Chang's completely unprompted 'Red Shoe Diaries' riff and 'I have a thing for butt stuff' seem to be movie riff contributions that have crossed a line.
jokes.explanation: Chang's 'I think you know I have a thing for butt stuff' is delivered presumably to the group with no context — a Chang non-sequitur that lands as over-sharing. The transition from the Annie/Troy confrontation to celebration is fast and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: To our success! We did it, guys. We actually pulled it off.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Vaughn is McConaughty-gross.

jokes.text: To Annie's inevitable breakup with Grodie J. McConaughey.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Britta toast their successful manipulation.
jokes.punchline: 'Grodie J. McConaughey' as a nickname for Vaughn — combining 'grodie' (gross) with Matthew McConaughey's shirtless hippie persona.
jokes.explanation: 'Grodie J. McConaughey' is an inspired coinage — the specific McConaughey reference captures the shirtless hippie type exactly, and 'Grodie J.' as the first/middle name is a perfect touch. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I was going to say something much darker.

jokes.text: Why would you say that? / Come on. You know that babies are extra cute when the parents are... / Both cute?
jokes.setup: Britta mentions cute babies; Jeff objects, then trails off at '...when the parents are—'
jokes.punchline: Britta finishes with 'Both cute?' — as a self-consciously innocent completion, but the unfinished sentence implies Jeff was about to say something about race (a Black/white interracial couple). The awkward pause IS the joke.
jokes.explanation: One of the most sophisticated jokes in the episode. The comedy is entirely in the gap — what Jeff was about to say, the pause as he realizes it, and Britta's perfectly innocent completion that lets them both pretend he wasn't about to say something about race. The structure is immaculate: set up with the babies comment, the unfinished sentence creates the tension, the pause IS the joke, and 'Both cute?' resolves it with plausible deniability. This is craft-forward comedy at its best.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You two are so manipulative! And before you ask, yes, that was sarcasm. I have to explain these things to you because you're both too dumb to understand subtext.

jokes.text: Do you want kids? / We'll see. / Put on something nice and find me after lunch.
jokes.setup: Following the babies awkwardness, Britta asks Jeff if he wants kids.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'We'll see' followed by 'Put on something nice and find me after lunch' — treating Britta's sincere question as a prelude to a hookup proposition.
jokes.explanation: 'Put on something nice and find me after lunch' is a great Jeff line — suave, presumptuous, slightly absurd given they're at Greendale. His pivot from 'babies' to treating Britta as a date prospect in two beats is very Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm sorry, I didn't realize you were suddenly so confident. You know what? I preferred it when you had low self-esteem. At least then you weren't so annoying about being smart.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's not... that's not even sarcasm, Troy. That's just being mean.

jokes.text: Hey, guys, thanks for getting involved in my love life. That was super cool and mature of you. / Oh, and since you're both clearly idiots, I should probably let you know that I'm being sarcastic.
jokes.setup: Annie confronts Jeff and Britta about their manipulation.
jokes.punchline: Annie's addition — 'since you're both clearly idiots, I should probably let you know that I'm being sarcastic' — is both a character moment (Annie's earnest need to be clear) and a meta-commentary on over-explaining jokes.
jokes.explanation: Annie explaining her own sarcasm is very true to her character — she's earnest enough that even her anger has an educational component. It's also self-aware about the show's audience. The double-layer (sarcasm + explanation of sarcasm) is well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh, thank you so much for that.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Yeah, really appreciate it.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: And while we're at it, why does the cafeteria keep running out of chocolate milk by noon?

jokes.text: Hey, guys, thanks for taking ugly Annie out of the palm of my hand and turning her into yet another hottie that will never get with me.
jokes.setup: Troy arrives with his own complaint to register about Jeff and Britta's scheme.
jokes.punchline: Troy's grievance is entirely selfish — they made Annie more attractive to him by telling him she was attractive, and now she's angry and unavailable. His complaint mimics Annie's format but for the wrong reasons.
jokes.explanation: Troy's complaint is structurally identical to Annie's but completely self-centered — his anger is that Annie is now off-limits to him. The 'ugly Annie' vs. 'hottie Annie' framing and 'palm of my hand' (implying he had a chance before Jeff intervened) is funny and very Troy. Good parallel structure with the previous beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: This macaroni is stale.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Nobody cares, Leonard.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, how did you know I bought this macaroni three weeks ago?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's... that's really disturbing.

jokes.text: Hey, guys, thanks for eating all the macaroni. / Shut up, Leonard, nobody even knows what you're talking about. / [Beat] I did eat all the macaroni. It's messed up that he knows.
jokes.setup: Leonard, a minor recurring character, inserts himself into the 'thanks for...' complaint format with a completely unrelated grievance.
jokes.punchline: Jeff dismisses Leonard; then aside admits 'I did eat all the macaroni. It's messed up that he knows.' — the reversal is that Jeff's dismissal was actually a cover-up.
jokes.explanation: Perfect three-beat structure. Leonard enters, makes a seemingly absurd non-sequitur complaint; Jeff dismisses him publicly; then privately to the audience admits guilty. The reversal is complete — Leonard was RIGHT. 'It's messed up that he knows' adds paranoia to the guilt. This is excellent joke structure with a perfect button. Leonard's peripheral complaint being the most accurate grievance in the scene is a great subversion.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: My father used to take me to see Runaway when I was a boy. Before the accident.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What accident?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: The one where he lost his legs. And his will to live. We'd sit in the theater, and for two hours, he'd forget about the pain. Runaway was his favorite. He died during the opening credits of Kickpuncher.

jokes.text: Actually, we decided to watch Runaway instead. Tom Selleck fights mechanical spiders.
jokes.setup: Everyone gathers for Kickpuncher 2 night.
jokes.punchline: Britta has unilaterally pivoted to a different movie — 'Tom Selleck fights mechanical spiders' — which is both a real movie and an immediately better premise.
jokes.explanation: 'Tom Selleck fights mechanical spiders' as a movie description is inherently funny and also accurately describes Runaway (1984). The pivot undermines Pierce's big preparation and sets up the spider bit to follow.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Change? Did you say change? Well, I'm all about change. I change my underwear every day. I change the channel when something boring comes on. I even change my mind sometimes. But you know what I never change? My position on Obama.

jokes.text: No, no, you can't do that. We just watched Kickpuncher, we have to see Kickpuncher 2. I have so many unanswered questions.
jokes.setup: Pierce has been preparing elaborate jokes for Kickpuncher 2 all week.
jokes.punchline: 'I have so many unanswered questions' — treating Kickpuncher as a serious narrative with unresolved plot threads requiring resolution.
jokes.explanation: Pierce's investment in Kickpuncher as serious cinema — 'unanswered questions' — is funny. The implied questions about a movie called Kickpuncher are inherently absurd. Good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm just naturally brilliant at movie jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You're delivering them at an unnatural rapid-fire pace. That's a stylistic choice, not brilliance.

jokes.text: My brother died on the set of that movie. / One of the mechanical spiders just went haywire and tore him to pieces. / And Tom Selleck just stood there. / He just stood there and watched him die.
jokes.setup: Everyone wants to watch the Tom Selleck spider movie. Pierce objects.
jokes.punchline: Pierce's objection is not about the movie quality but a devastating personal tragedy — his brother was killed on set by a mechanical spider, and Tom Selleck's witnessed the death and did nothing.
jokes.explanation: One of the absolute best jokes in the episode and potentially the season. The structure is immaculate: escalates from mechanical spider malfunction to torn-to-pieces to the devastating final detail — 'Tom Selleck just stood there.' The indictment of Tom Selleck as a passive witness to this horrific event is absurdist perfection. The repetition 'He just stood there and watched him die' compounds the accusation. This achieves the rare thing of being both completely absurd and emotionally resonant. Extremely quotable, high craft, perfect character delivery for Pierce — only he would have this specific, ridiculous, devastating backstory.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You know what? You're so lame, even I notice.

jokes.text: Okay, then, let's watch your Kickpuncher 2. / Yeah. Okay. / Sorry for your loss. / Yeah. That's messed up, dude.
jokes.setup: Pierce has just told the group his brother was killed by a mechanical spider while Tom Selleck watched.
jokes.punchline: Everyone immediately accepts his trauma as a valid reason to change the movie, and their condolences are brief and generic — the mundane comfort ('sorry for your loss') against an insane story.
jokes.explanation: The group's immediate acceptance — dropping the Tom Selleck movie without question — and their generic condolences ('sorry for your loss' / 'that's messed up') against the insane story is perfect deadpan. Nobody questions the story. That's the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, maybe I was preparing jokes, but that's better than you people just making fun of me all the time without any material or preparation whatsoever. At least I'm trying. You guys just wing it and hope something lands. That's not comedy, that's just being mean.

jokes.text: My punches were only as strong as my punches. / And then things changed. / Change? Time to change the channel.
jokes.setup: Movie sequel's opening narration sets up Kickpuncher 2's premise.
jokes.punchline: Pierce riffs on 'change' — a pun on 'change the channel.'
jokes.explanation: Pierce's first riff of the new night — a simple word pun on 'change' — is mediocre, which is intentional. He's warming up and still not very good.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm tired of all of you judging me. At least I didn't grow up in a cardboard box like some people. Oh wait, Chang, that explains SO much about you.

jokes.text: This guy's gonna be begging for change if he keeps making movies this bad.
jokes.setup: Movie narration says 'change'; Pierce made the channel-change pun.
jokes.punchline: Jeff extends the 'change' riff by pivoting to 'begging for change' — implying the director will be broke.
jokes.explanation: One layer deeper than Pierce's riff — building on the pun rather than just using it once. Functional movie riffing.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, my mother was a very sick woman.

jokes.text: They should change this movie to something good. / This movie stinks, we better change its diaper. / That's change we can believe in.
jokes.setup: The 'change' riff has started and everyone is piling on.
jokes.punchline: Three more 'change' puns in quick succession — 'change to something good' / 'change its diaper' / 'that's change we can believe in' (Obama reference). The escalating badness of the puns is itself the joke.
jokes.explanation: 'Change its diaper' is the best of the three — specific and absurd. 'That's change we can believe in' is an Obama reference that's become dated but lands as Pierce's attempt at topicality. The pile-on structure is intentionally about quantity rather than quality.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Why did the chicken cross the road? To get to the— *falls*

dialogue.speaker: Everyone
dialogue.line: *laughs uncontrollably*

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: And that's how you kill in comedy.

jokes.text: Okay, obviously something strange is happening here. / What do you mean? I'm making jokes during a movie. / Yeah, but you're doing it with the speed and determination of the incomparable Robin Williams.
jokes.setup: Pierce has been riffing with unusual speed and volume.
jokes.punchline: Jeff diagnoses Pierce as performing like 'the incomparable Robin Williams' — meaning the riffs are coming too fast and too confidently for someone who was struggling yesterday.
jokes.explanation: 'The incomparable Robin Williams' as the standard for someone riffing too fast is a good specific reference. Jeff's detective work — recognizing over-preparation — is true to his character as the most perceptive person in the group.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm okay, I'm okay. Now, why did the chicken cross the road? To get to the other side!

jokes.text: Yeah. Maybe I'm just that brilliant. / I think you came prepared. / Dude, even I know you're lame. And I'm a tenured professor sitting in a beanbag chair.
jokes.setup: Pierce is accused of pre-writing his jokes.
jokes.punchline: Chang's self-aware interjection — 'Even I know you're lame. And I'm a tenured professor sitting in a beanbag chair' — a devastating self-roast that makes his insult credible by acknowledging his own absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Chang's line is excellent — 'Even I know you're lame' acknowledges his own compromised position as a standard, and 'tenured professor sitting in a beanbag chair' as his self-description is a perfect, specific image of his professional decline. The self-deprecation that strengthens the insult is sophisticated comedy writing.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You can't just waltz in here and be our mom. And those mom jeans? They're doing you no favors.

jokes.text: You're not a professor. / Shut up, man.
jokes.setup: Chang claims to be a tenured professor.
jokes.punchline: Jeff corrects him (Chang's credentials are questionable); Chang's 'Shut up, man' is defensive and petulant.
jokes.explanation: Quick, tight beat. 'Shut up, man' as Chang's entire defense is good deflation. The two-word punchline works well.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I didn't enjoy it. It was... it was nothing. Completely unremarkable. Her lips were just regular lips. Soft, but in a normal way. Not special. I've kissed lots of people with lips just like that. Identical lips, really. And the kiss itself was just a kiss. A regular kiss. No spark, no chemistry, no reason to ever think about it again, which I won't. I'm not thinking about it now.

jokes.text: Fine, you got me. I did a little advanced work. / Pathetic? No. I'll tell you what's pathetic. You all sitting here making fun of other people's work. You don't feel good about yourselves so you have to tear down everything around you.
jokes.setup: Pierce admits to pre-writing his jokes, then immediately pivots to a speech about how everyone else is pathetic.
jokes.punchline: The deflection — turning a genuine busted-cheating moment into a philosophical accusation against everyone else — is both self-serving and somewhat accurate.
jokes.explanation: Pierce's pivot from 'you caught me' to 'you're all pathetic anyway' is perfectly in character — he can't take accountability without redirecting blame. The speech actually has a point (they DO mock other people's work) which makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm not attracted to Annie. I don't even think about her like that.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Really? Because I remember you describing her as 'petite, cute nose, those eyes that make you want to protect her.'

jokes.text: What's the matter? Mama Chang didn't breastfeed? / She read in a book that it wouldn't make a difference.
jokes.setup: Pierce turns his speech on Chang specifically with a 'mama' joke.
jokes.punchline: Chang responds with detailed, deadpan information about his mother's child-rearing research — confirming the specific accusation accidentally.
jokes.explanation: Pierce's 'mama' insult is a rhetorical device; Chang's literal, clinical confirmation that his mother did in fact consult a book and decline breastfeeding is devastating. Chang accidentally validating Pierce's insult with specific sourcing ('she read in a book') is a perfect non-sequitur-as-confirmation structure.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Does anyone get specific about me?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I may have sent you some emails that were a little too specific.

jokes.text: Pierce, that was deep. / And total BS. Yeah, this isn't about us. This is a deflection because you can't get a genuine laugh. / Mm-hm. That, in itself, is a laugh.
jokes.setup: Pierce has delivered his speech about the group tearing things down.
jokes.punchline: Jeff diagnoses it as a deflection; Pierce's 'That, in itself, is a laugh' — claiming that being caught in a deflection is ITSELF comedy.
jokes.explanation: Pierce claiming his busted manipulative deflection counts as comedy is a clever meta-move — he's trying to claim credit for being caught. It's both self-serving and weirdly correct (it did get a laugh in the narrative).

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Pierce, I'm gonna need you to stop hitting 'reply all' on your feelings.

jokes.text: I know I'm funny and I don't need any of you people to validate me. / [He trips and falls.] Oh! / Biggest laugh of the night. / Yes, it was. Totally.
jokes.setup: Pierce declares his independence from the group's approval and storms out.
jokes.punchline: He immediately trips and falls, which the group agrees is the funniest thing he's done all night.
jokes.explanation: Classic slapstick with perfect thematic timing — Pierce exits with a declaration of comedic independence and immediately demonstrates that physical comedy is his best mode. 'Biggest laugh of the night' as the group's consensus is a good button. The tripping isn't original but the placement and payoff are excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I'm going to mark you as spam.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Spam? Pam? I don't even know a Pam!

jokes.text: Then I was going to say, 'It's a good day to be gay.'
jokes.setup: Pierce delivers his triumphant exit line after the accidental fall got the biggest laugh.
jokes.punchline: He attempts to rehabilitate his prepared material by claiming the fall was a setup for the gay joke — an obvious, desperate lie.
jokes.explanation: Pierce retroactively claiming his pratfall was a deliberate setup for the gay joke is a perfect character beat — he can't accept accidental success without trying to own it. The callback to the Chang-praised joke is tight.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We're like the Brady Bunch, except instead of living together in a house, we're living together in a community college, and instead of having wholesome adventures, we're dealing with real-life drama and dysfunction.

jokes.text: You're not my mom, Britta. She would never wear boots that go up that high.
jokes.setup: Britta claims to be like Annie's mother.
jokes.punchline: Annie's rejection includes a specific, petty detail about Britta's boots — 'that go up that high' — implying they're inappropriately sexy for a maternal figure.
jokes.explanation: Very sharp line. Annie's rebuttal to Britta's maternal claim goes straight to wardrobe — 'boots that go up that high' is a perfect specific detail implying Britta dresses too provocatively to be a mother figure. It's also Annie being both sharp and somewhat prudish. Great character integration for both characters.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I would never say that! I don't use that kind of language!

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: But if I did, it would be because it's a very nice butt.

jokes.text: I'm not Juno, okay, homeslice?
jokes.setup: Britta admits she's not cool enough to handle her ex with someone she knows.
jokes.punchline: 'I'm not Juno' — referencing the 2007 film character who is unrealistically chill about everything — while using 'homeslice' (Juno's affected slang), which undermines the rejection of the comparison.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant self-undermining joke — Britta says 'I'm not Juno' while using Juno's specific slang ('homeslice'), which immediately contradicts her claim. The pop culture reference is sharp and specific rather than generic name-dropping; it's character-defining. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: It's not weird.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's not weird.

jokes.text: What are you insinuating? / I took that kiss for the team. / What? / Yeah. That kiss wasn't for pleasure. It was strategic and joyless.
jokes.setup: Annie accuses Jeff of being jealous about Britta and Vaughn; Jeff denies having any personal interest in Britta.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's claim that his kiss with Britta was 'strategic and joyless' — a desperate overcorrection that reveals far more than a simple 'we're just friends' would have.
jokes.explanation: 'Strategic and joyless' is an excellent line — Jeff is so committed to denying attraction that he characterizes a romantic moment as a military operation. The overspecificity ('joyless' is a strange detail if it truly meant nothing) betrays him completely. Very Jeff. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, let's be honest here. We're all potential romantic options for each other.

jokes.text: You did get weirdly specific when you were describing Annie's body.
jokes.setup: Jeff claims his interest is not personal; Britta calls out his behavior during the manipulation scene.
jokes.punchline: Britta pointing out that Jeff was 'weirdly specific' about Annie's body when describing her to Troy — turning Jeff's earlier manipulation against him.
jokes.explanation: Britta's callback to Jeff's earlier behavior is well-constructed — she uses his own actions as evidence against him. 'Weirdly specific' is a good characterization that the audience would agree with.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: I didn't get any of your messages, Annie. My phone broke, so I threw it in the river as a symbol of my freedom from technology.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: But then I realized my car keys were in the waterproof case attached to it.

jokes.text: More specific than the stuff you told me about Britta? / What?
jokes.setup: Britta has accused Jeff of being too specific about Annie's body.
jokes.punchline: Annie reveals Jeff apparently told her specific things about Britta too — suggesting a whole web of private admissions nobody knew about.
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation — Annie's reveal that Jeff discussed Britta's body with her as well detonates the whole 'I'm not interested' argument. The structure builds from one accusation to a cascade. Britta's 'What?' is the right reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: After elaborate romantic lyrics complimenting Annie's eyes, smile, and heart, he concludes: 'And baby, your left elbow is absolutely magnificent.'

jokes.text: Does anyone get specific about me? / Check your e-mail. / I marked you as spam. / Who the hell is Pam?
jokes.setup: Shirley asks if anyone has discussed her body.
jokes.punchline: Abed says 'check your e-mail' — implying he sent something; Shirley says she marked it as spam; Abed's 'Who the hell is Pam?' — apparently confusing Shirley with someone named Pam is both an insult and a reveal that Abed has limited investment in learning people's names.
jokes.explanation: Four-line exchange with great escalation. 'Check your e-mail' implies Abed has prepared. 'I marked you as spam' is Shirley's inadvertent admission that she doesn't want to hear from him. 'Who the hell is Pam?' is a perfect button — Abed doesn't even know her name but was apparently discussing her attractiveness.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: A song about liking Annie's nose? That's not even a song. That's just saying something you like and then singing it badly.

jokes.text: When you guys first came in, we were as wholesome and healthy as the family in Brady Bunch. And now we're as dysfunctional and incestuous as the cast of The Brady Bunch.
jokes.setup: The group's web of romantic jealousies and manipulations has been exposed.
jokes.punchline: Abed distinguishes between the Brady Bunch as a fictional family and the Brady Bunch cast in reality — using the actual real-world drama of that show's cast as his reference for dysfunction and 'incest' (relationships between cast members).
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines of the episode and a classic Abed moment. The distinction between 'family in Brady Bunch' and 'cast of The Brady Bunch' is a genuinely clever and well-sourced observation (the Brady Bunch cast had real romantic entanglements). Only Abed would have this specific pop-culture knowledge and apply it this precisely. The structure — setup matching both clauses with 'Brady Bunch' but different referents — is immaculate. Extremely quotable. This is what the show does best: meta-commentary through Abed that is also genuinely insightful.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Vaughn and I are going to have a romantic evening. We're going to go to the park, lie on a blanket, and count clouds.

jokes.text: No more creepy than when Jeff wears tight jeans and you say, 'I'd like to slap those buns on the grill.'
jokes.setup: Shirley says the group's romantic entanglements are 'creepy.'
jokes.punchline: Annie exposes Shirley's private commentary about Jeff's physique — 'slap those buns on the grill' — using it to deflect Shirley's moral high ground.
